match.reason: None of the bank points teaches the distinction between clauses and phrases; the closest, the simple, compound and complex sentences point, only defines a clause as a group with a verb and never covers phrases or the requirement for a subject.

draft.title: Clauses and phrases
card: a group of words with a subject and a verb. The subject is who or what does the action, and the verb is the action or state. In "Mia sang", Mia is the subject and sang is the verb.
a group of words that does not have both a subject and a verb. "After lunch" and "the tall boy" are phrases.
a clause that makes sense on its own. "The bus arrived" is a main clause.
a clause that depends on a main clause and does not make sense alone. In "The bus arrived when the rain stopped", "when the rain stopped" is subordinate.
draft.remember: A clause has a subject and a verb. A phrase does not have both.

a.q: Which group of words is a clause?
a.why: "The dog barked" has a subject, the dog, and a verb, barked. The other three have no subject and verb together, so they are phrases. "Barking loudly at night" is tempting, but it has no subject.
a.clue: Look for who or what, plus an action.

b.q: Read: "Leo packed his bag before the bell rang." Which words are a subordinate clause?
b.why: "Before the bell rang" has a subject, the bell, and a verb, rang, but it depends on the main clause and does not make sense alone. "Before the bell" is only a phrase, because it has no verb.
b.clue: Find the words with their own subject and verb that cannot stand alone.
